The vote asks the President of the General Assembly to form a group of three people, himself among them. The group must find the base on which a sound cease-fire in Korea can be struck. The need to gather and weigh facts on atomic radiation grows, the text holds, as the stock of such facts grows in size and range. un-sc-res-84:

Member states had been urged to give the Republic such aid as it needed to throw back the attack and restore peace in the area.

The prompt and strong aid of states and peoples is welcomed. States that send forces are urged to place them under a single command. That command would be led by the United States, whose flag the force would fly beside the UN's own. Reports on the course of the war must come back to the Council. So began the U.S.-led UN war in Korea.

frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d84: Chiang Kai-shek wrote to Roosevelt on November 2, 1943, three weeks before their Cairo meeting. The letter is Document 84 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d184:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt a brief, most-secret telegram from Moscow on 2 November 1943. Hull was in the Soviet capital for talks with British and Soviet leaders. The message was unnumbered, marked for the President only, and sent through Army channels.

Only a fragment appears here: one short line about the Far East after Germany's defeat, noted as the end of a message sent in another code. Hull asked Roosevelt to flash an acknowledgement back to him at Cairo. A reply bearing Roosevelt's typed name sits in his papers, though the editors note it may never actually have been sent.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d284:
A note by the secretaries of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, numbered J.C.S. 606, was circulated at Cairo on 22 November 1943. Signed by F. B. Royal and A. J. McFarland of the Joint Secretariat, it passes on a suggestion from General Deane, the American military envoy in Moscow, relayed by radio to General Marshall.

Deane proposes that the chiefs put the Russians on the defensive at once by arriving at Tehran with requests of their own, rather than spending the meeting doing all the explaining. His suggested subjects are air bases, better communications and weather exchange, shuttle bomber bases, and coordinating timing with Overlord. Marshall submitted the paragraph to the Joint Chiefs for their consideration.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d384:
Foreign Commissar Molotov sent President Roosevelt a short formal note at Tehran on 28 November 1943. It is printed here in Charles Bohlen's translation from the Russian. The original has not been found. It concerns the Cairo communiqué, whose text had been shared with the Soviet side.

Marshal Stalin, Molotov writes, has acquainted himself with the communiqué on the North Africa conference of Roosevelt, Chiang Kai-shek, and Churchill, held in the second half of November. Stalin expresses his thanks for the information and states that he has no observation at all to make on the communiqué. The editors add a cross-reference to Stalin's oral comments on the statement, given at the Tehran luncheon of 30 November and printed later in the volume.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d484:
Staff planners working under the Combined Chiefs of Staff delivered this report on December 5, 1943, during the Second Cairo Conference. The Combined Staff Planners were American and British officers who tested plans against hard facts about troops, ships, and supplies. The State Department printed the report in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Planning reports did the quiet arithmetic of the alliance. Before the chiefs could recommend a course, the planners had to show it could actually be done, and at what cost to other theaters. A reader studying how Cairo's decisions were reached will find this layer essential, because it shows which options survived contact with the numbers.
frus-1944-quebec-d84:
Harry Hopkins wrote to Secretary of State Hull on September 5, 1944. Hopkins served as President Roosevelt's special assistant. The State Department printed his message in the Quebec 1944 volume. It belongs to the last week of summit preparation.

Hopkins worked as the President's personal link to many officials. A note from him to Hull carried weight beyond its length. The Quebec Conference opened one week later in Canada. Staff channels like this one kept departments aligned before it began. For readers, the message shows quiet coordination at the highest level. It happened while public attention stayed on the armies in France.
frus-1944-quebec-d184:
Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on the morning of September 14, 1944, proposing to bring Richard Law, and perhaps Eden, to call at 11 a.m. The subject was applying UNRRA, the relief agency, to Italy. In the event only Law accompanied him, and the editors found no further information about what was said at the meeting.

The note quotes historian Llewellyn Woodward on the British purpose. Churchill had taken great trouble, Woodward wrote, to put proposals for easing Italy's situation before the president at Quebec, ahead of the American presidential election. Britain expected its views to get consideration from the State Department. A joint statement on Italy was later tentatively agreed at Hyde Park.
frus-1944-quebec-d284: A one-paragraph minute of September 15, 1944, records agreement between Roosevelt and Churchill on major war criminals. frus-1945-malta-yalta-d84:
Stalin replied to Roosevelt on 27 December 1944, and the voting plan hit its wall. His top secret message answers the proposal Harriman had delivered on 14 December. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

Stalin fully agrees that the questions left open at Dumbarton Oaks must be settled before a United Nations conference, voting first of all. The first two points of Roosevelt's proposal, he says, meet no objections and can be accepted. The third point is different. With regret, he sees no possibility of agreeing to its wording, because it weakens the rule that the permanent members must act in unanimity.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d184:
A British caller's hurt feelings fill this record of a talk on 6 December 1944. Stettinius's memorandum of conversation, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, describes Michael Wright's late-afternoon visit. Halifax had gone to New York to speak, and Wright came in his place.

Wright said he had been much hurt by the Secretary's statement on Italy, and that it had caused great embarrassment. The prime minister and Eden were aroused, and a Commons debate on Greece loomed on Friday. London feared that the statement's words on other freed countries were aimed at Greece as well. Wright then read a one-page personal message from Eden, too personal to leave behind. Eden wrote that the British were surprised and hurt by so damaging a statement.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d284:
Malta's agenda, day by day, is proposed in this British paper of 25 January 1945. Numbered C. C. S. 765/8, it is titled “Agenda for the Next U. S.-British Staff Conference” and is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. London suggests settling the order of business before the American chiefs leave Washington.

For the war against Germany, the talks open on strategy in northwest Europe, with Eisenhower in discussion. A draft directive to the Supreme Commander, tabled by the British, follows. Then comes the Mediterranean, with Field Marshal Alexander, and a draft directive for his command. Coordination across the three European fronts, bomblines and air liaison with the Russians, the U-boat threat, and the combined bomber offensive fill the list. A planning date for the end of the German war closes the first part.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d384:
Hiss's pencil raced at the foreign ministers' session of February 8, 1945, where Eden chaired. Two questions on the world body had been sent down. Should two or three Soviet republics hold seats? And when and where should the founding conference meet? Stettinius rose to invite the great allies to a conference in the United States.

He hoped the President had not shocked anyone by naming March. The time could fit the convenience of Molotov and Eden. Still, the Americans wanted the earliest possible date, perhaps the latter part of April. Who would be invited came next. Hiss's broken lines carry the birth notices of the San Francisco conference.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d484:
Ambassador Winant wrote past the Secretary of State, straight to the President, on February 7, 1945 — and said why. Eden, who directed Britain's man on the European Advisory Commission, and Ambassador Gusev, Russia's member, were both at the conference. Winant, left out of it, chose to report in person.

His news was that all three powers had approved, without reserve, the surrender instrument, the zones protocol, and the control machinery pact for Germany. If that machinery was to work, he argued, broader accords would still be needed. The letter's edge is plain: the man who built the occupation texts in London was watching Yalta from outside.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d84:
Edward Page recorded a turning point in the access fight in a Moscow memorandum dated June 21, 1945. The memo is document 84 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Ambassador Harriman met Vyshinsky, who handed over a written reply about the American advance group waiting to enter Berlin.

Vyshinsky explained that the delay came from Zhukov being in Moscow until June 28. But if Washington wished to start without him, it could send its group whenever it liked. He also shared the first firm site plans. Each delegation would get its own zone, as at Yalta. And since Berlin was destroyed, the conference would sit at Babelsberg near Potsdam, in the Crown Prince's palace. The Americans had their opening at last.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d184:
British Minister John Balfour proposed two United Nations items for the agenda in a letter dated July 5, 1945. The letter to Matthews, with its enclosure, is document 184 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The new world organization was still being set up, and its first posts were unfilled.

London wants the leaders to settle two posts before that body meets in early August. One is who chairs the Executive Committee. The other is who serves as Executive Secretary of the Preparatory Commission. Agreeing among the Big Three first would let France and China be approached by month's end. The enclosure also proposes an early exchange of views on where the world organization should have its seat. But no final decision should be taken at Terminal, since other countries' views must count.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d284:
John Erhardt, the political adviser for Austrian affairs, reported the planned entry into Vienna in a telegram from Florence on July 15, 1945. The message is document 284 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. General Clark had left for Brazil and would return July 26.

In Clark's absence, Erhardt reports, the deputy commanders are to confer with Soviet officers in Vienna to settle the details for taking over the national sectors. The Berlin entry taught the need for careful planning and full agreement first. The talks will be purely military, with no political advisers present. If the zones and control agreements are ratified by July 26, the American, British, and French commanders, with their political advisers, hope to enter Vienna soon after and remain there permanently.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d384:
Joint control of German external assets is pressed in a Washington memorandum by Oliver, acting chief of the Division of Economic Security Controls, dated July 7, 1945. It was written for Collado and Despres, the Department's economic officers. American policy, Oliver states, was to control German assets abroad, and to make that control a joint one, headed by the Allied Control Council.

It would be most unfortunate, he argues, if control fell to zone commanders alone, wherever the parent firms or marks of ownership happened to sit. A common policy had to be pressed for. The memo then lists the problems in the way of agreement among the occupying powers.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d484:
Recognition of Poland's new government moves forward in Grew's cable to Harriman of June 22, 1945. The Department concurs, Grew writes, in Harriman's action as commissioner in accepting the settlement reached in Moscow. For his information, he has telegraphed the President an outline of Harriman's message of June 21 on the agreement on the Polish government.

In that telegram Grew recommended that the President look favorably, if the British government concurs, on granting recognition to the newly constituted government. It would be recognized as the new Polish Provisional Government of National Unity. As soon as he hears from the President, Grew promises, he will inform Harriman of the decision.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d584:

Stephen C. Meyer, a leading advocate of intelligent design, joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2008. Meyer argues that life's complexity points to a mind behind nature, a claim mainstream science rejects. Rogan hosts the case at full length, as he often does with dissenters.

Meyer lays out his best-known points, from the sudden spread of animal forms in the fossil record to the code-like nature of DNA. Rogan asks how the idea differs from plain creationism and where its proof is thin. The episode is a clear statement of the design case, useful for anyone who wants it from its own side.
abbott-flatland-1884:
Edwin A Abbott, an English schoolmaster and theologian, published Flatland in 1884 under the name 'A Square.' The short novel is set in a world of only two dimensions. It is the founding work of fiction about higher dimensions and a sharp satire of Victorian society.

The Square tells how Flatland's classes are ranked by shape, from lowly lines to priestly circles. A visit from a Sphere of three dimensions blows his mind open to worlds beyond his own. Abbott uses the tale to teach geometry and to mock rank, dogma, and fear of new ideas.
nadaillac-prehistoric-america-1884:
The Marquis de Nadaillac, a French scholar of prehistory, published Pre-historic America in 1884. He gathered what Europeans then knew about the deep past of the New World. Mound-builders, cliff-dwellers, and cave finds all pass through his survey.

Nadaillac weighs how long people had lived in the Americas and what they left behind. He writes as a well-read Victorian synthesizer rather than a field digger. Much has been superseded by later archaeology. The book remains a clear window onto nineteenth-century thinking about America's first peoples. French readers received here one of the first broad surveys of the subject.
jacko-ape-man-yale-british-colonist-1884:
A Victoria newspaper told British Columbia a strange tale on July 4, 1884. The Daily British Colonist reported a creature called Jacko, caught by a train crew above Yale. The headline asked what the thing was, and the report calls it a kind of gorilla.

Jacko was small, hairy, and strong, the crew said, and was kept in town for show. No trace of him stands past the news reports of that summer. Most now take the tale for a hoax or a tall yarn of the rails. Still, the report is read as the first draft of the Bigfoot legend.
mars-exploration-remote-viewing-1984:
A remote viewer sat in a plain room in 1984 and described Mars as it was a million years past. The session transcript of May 22, 1984, freed from the STAR GATE files, is that record in full. A monitor fed the viewer map coordinates and took the words down as they came.

The viewer tells of pyramids, a dying race, storms of dust, and a world in its last age. The tale reads like science fiction stamped and filed as spy work. It is the most famed single session of the whole program. No file shows the remote viewing faith at full stretch like this one.
britten-nineteenth-century-miracles-1884:
Emma Hardinge Britten swept the globe for marvels in Nineteenth Century Miracles, her vast book of 1884. Her faith held that the dead speak and heal in her age. She set out to prove it with tales from land past land, faith past faith, town past town.

Each part gives names, dates, and sworn tales of cures and ghosts. The sheer bulk is her case. She meant the book as a store of proof no foe could shrug off. It is the faith's world tour in one tome. She knew the chief names of the faith at first hand in her tours. That close reach gives her vast claims a weight mere hearsay lacks.
collins-idyll-of-the-white-lotus-1884:
A tale of old Egypt frames Mabel Collins's The Idyll of the White Lotus, her tale of 1884. A boy with sight past the veil is drawn to a shrine of the white lotus. Priests of two paths fight for his soul. One path serves self and rite. One serves the hid light.

Collins wove her creed into tale form here. The book charmed fans who found dry creed hard. It grew to be the creed's best loved tale of the path. Its soft glow still wins new fans each year. A sage of the creed is said to have blessed the tale in draft. Fans took that nod as proof its lore rang true and deep.
stephens-handbook-old-northern-runic-188:
George Stephens, an English scholar who worked in Denmark, made this guide to the old rune stones in 1884. It covers carved stones and other rune works from Scandinavia and from England. Stephens spent years on trips to read the stones in place.

The guide gives drawings of the stones, reads their texts, and tells where each one stands. It sorts the signs by age and land so the reader can trace how the script changed. For its time it was the main English book on the rune stones of the north.
cavendish-experiments-on-air-1784:
Henry Cavendish, a rich and shy English scholar, read these papers on air in 1784 and 1785. He was famed for the care and truth of his trials. His work bore on the great fight over phlogiston that then split chemistry. Few trials of that age can match his for care, and few men hid from fame as he did.

Cavendish joined two gases with a spark and got pure water, weight for weight. The result showed water is a compound, not a base stuff as men had long held. He also wrote back to Kirwan in the same work. The proof shook the old scheme hard.
owen-antiquity-of-man-1884:
Richard Owen, the great English master of bones, gave his late word on man's age in this book of 1884. Its spark was a human frame dug from the Thames bank at Tilbury. Owen was old, and his fame as the chief judge of such finds stood high.

He sets out the frame bone by bone and weighs how old it may be. His word counts, since for years his no had held back claims of deep age for man. The book is the old master's last word on a theme that had moved past him.
bruno-de-infinito-1584:
Giordano Bruno wrote these talks in Italian in 1584, while he lived in London. The full title speaks of the vast whole, the world, and the worlds. Bruno held that the stars are suns with worlds of their own. The Church later burned him at the stake in Rome.

Five talks pit Bruno's voice against men who cling to the old closed cosmos. He says space has no edge and no core point. Earth is one world among a vast host of worlds. The book is a root text for the claim that life fills the sky.
sbe-21-saddharma-pundarika-1884:
H. Kern gave the Saddharma-Pundarika English dress in 1884. The work is Book Twenty-One of the Sacred Books of the East. Its short name in the West is the Lotus Sutra. The Lotus is one of the great texts of the Mahayana faith.

The Buddha tells tales of skill in means: how one path serves all kinds of men. A lost son, a burning house, and a rain that falls on all grass form famed tales. The text holds that all beings may reach full Buddhahood in time. Kern's dress was the first full one in English.
twain-huckleberry-finn-1884:
Mark Twain published Adventures of Huckleberry Finn in 1884, complete in the first edition text. Many call it the great American novel, the book modern American writing starts from in earnest. Twain set it in the slaveholding South of his own boyhood on the Mississippi River.

Huck, fleeing his drunk father's beatings, fakes his death and takes to the river. Jim, fleeing slavery, joins him on a raft down the wide Mississippi at night. Feuding families, con men, and a lynch mob test Huck's growing conscience on shore. He decides to help Jim though he believes it damns his soul to hell. Twain's vernacular voice and moral depth keep the book central and contested still.
pseudomonarchia-daemonum-weyer-scot-1584:
Johann Weyer's Pseudomonarchia Daemonum reached English in Reginald Scot's version of 1584. Scot printed it inside his Discoverie of Witchcraft, the first English text of Weyer's demon lore. Weyer, a Dutch physician, had listed the ranks of hell to mock credulous witch fears.

The catalogue names dukes, princes, and counts of hell, with their legions and seals. Each demon gets a rank, an office, and the hour to call him by name. Scot's larger book argues that most witch charges are fraud, pity, or cruel delusion among judges. His skepticism cost him favor, and King James later ordered his book burned in Scotland. The list still feeds grimoires and occult lore in print to this day.
strindberg-married-1884:
August Strindberg published Married in 1884, a story collection of twenty tales of marriage as war. The book got him prosecuted for blasphemy in Sweden for a passage on the sacrament in one tale. It was the scandal-book of 1880s Scandinavia, and its trial made Strindberg a national figure overnight there.

The tales show husbands and wives in trades of money, pride, faith, and thwarted love at home. Some are tender, most are acid, and all distrust the romantic gloss on wedded life in Sweden. A doll's house of his own, in one tale, answers Ibsen's Nora with a colder eye. He was acquitted, but the case and the book fixed his name as marriage's great accuser in print. English readers met here the prose fighter behind the later battle-of-the-sexes plays.
sienkiewicz-with-fire-and-sword-1884:
Henryk Sienkiewicz published With Fire and Sword in 1884, first volume of his immortal Trilogy of Poland's wars. The 1648 Cossack uprising is seen through the eyes of Polish knights in a vast historical epic. Sienkiewicz wrote to lift Polish hearts under foreign partition, and the Trilogy became Poland's national prose epic.

Jan Skrzetuski, a hussar envoy, loves Helena Kurcewiczówna and is swept into Bohdan Khmelnytsky's great Cossack rising of 1648. Zagłoba, the fat, witty old soldier, steals scene after scene with his stratagems, boasts, and unbreakable good cheer in camp. Tartars, sieges, and the sack of towns fill a canvas of steppe war in its full horror and dash. The defense of Zbaraż closes the volume in a siege Poles read as their Thermopylae of national memory in arms. Its sweep and color made Sienkiewicz, in time, a Nobel laureate.
huysmans-against-grain-1884:
Joris-Karl Huysmans published Against the Grain in 1884, a French novel with almost no plot in the usual sense. Its hero, Des Esseintes, is a rich and tired nobleman. He shuts himself away in a house outside Paris. There he surrounds himself with rare books, scents, jewels, and art.

Most of the book lists what Des Esseintes loves and what he hates. His tastes stand against the plain tastes of the world outside. The novel became a guide for the Decadent movement, which prized art and artifice over nature. Its strange hero still draws readers who like beauty pushed to an extreme.
spencer-man-versus-state-1884:
Herbert Spencer published The Man versus the State in 1884, a set of essays against expanding government. Spencer argues that new laws often repeat the harms of old controls. Each reform, he claims, breeds fresh coercion and fresh evils. The coming slavery is his warning phrase for a state that manages daily life.

He attacks state education, state charity, and regulation of trade and health. His ideal is a state limited to defense and the enforcement of contracts. The book became a classic statement of small-state liberal thought. American readers later took it up as a libertarian text. It shows Spencer in his most polemical mood.
parkman-montcalm-wolfe-1884:
Francis Parkman published Montcalm and Wolfe in 1884, the climax of his series France and England in North America. The book covers the Seven Years' War in America, ending at Quebec in 1759. Generals Montcalm and Wolfe, French and British, both die in the final battle. The fate of a continent turns on their contest.

Parkman worked from archives in France, Britain, and America for decades. Forests, forts, and snowbound campaigns fill his vivid narrative. His sympathies favor British order, yet he honors Montcalm's courage. The two volumes of this title close a life's work. Parkman remains America's great romantic historian of the frontier wars.
moody-prevailing-prayer-1884:
Dwight Moody was the great American revival preacher of the late nineteenth century, founder of schools and mass meetings across two continents. His Prevailing Prayer: What Hinders It, published in 1884, asks why so many prayers seem to go unanswered. It became the most widely read evangelical tract on prayer of its era.

Moody lists the hindrances plainly: cherished sin, cold hearts, haste, doubt, and prayers that ask only for selfish ends. He mixes short Bible lessons with stories from his own campaigns and converts. Revival-minded readers used the book as a checklist for clearing the way to answered prayer.
beal-buddhist-records-western-world-vol1:
Samuel Beal translated the Si-yu-ki, the record of the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang's journey to India, as Buddhist Records of the Western World. Volume one appeared in 1884. Xuanzang traveled from 629 to 645, crossing Central Asia to study at the great Indian monasteries.

The record describes kingdoms, roads, relics, and monasteries of seventh-century Asia in a pilgrim's faithful detail. Xuanzang names the doctrines he heard, the stupas he worshipped at, and the rulers who fed his party. Historians of India and China alike mine Beal's volumes for facts found nowhere else. Beal's notes name modern places for the pilgrim's ancient stops.
spinoza-chief-works-elwes-vol-2-1884:
Volume 2 of Elwes's Chief Works of Benedict de Spinoza appeared in 1884. Where Volume 1 held the political tracts, Volume 2 holds the heart of the system. It opens with On the Improvement of the Understanding, Spinoza's unfinished guide to clear thinking.

The Ethics follows, built in geometric order from definitions and axioms, treating God, nature, mind, and the passions. Spinoza argued that God and nature are one, and that freedom means understanding necessity. Select Letters close the volume, showing the system under discussion with friends and critics. In Elwes's Victorian English, this volume gave generations their Spinoza: austere, logical, and quietly radical about religion and the good life.
lanier-poems-1884:
Sidney Lanier died of tuberculosis in 1881 at thirty-nine, worn out by poverty and the illness he had carried since his Civil War prison days. His widow gathered his poems, and the posthumous collection appeared in 1884. It made the South's poet-flautist famous after his death.

The Marshes of Glynn, his greatest poem, moves through Georgia's salt marshes at sundown into a meditation on faith and freedom. The Symphony gives each instrument of the orchestra a voice against commerce and greed. Sunrise, Corn, and other lyrics show his musical line at full stretch. Lanier's verse sings even when it argues. The 1884 volume fixed his place as the leading Southern poet of his century.
schiller-love-and-intrigue-1784:
Love and Intrigue, known in German as Kabale und Liebe, is Schiller's tragedy of 1784, Englished in the Bohn Standard Library set. Ferdinand, a president's son, loves Luise, the daughter of a humble music teacher. Their love crosses the hard class line of a small German court.

The president plans a rich marriage for his son and plots to break the match. A forged letter poisons Ferdinand's trust and leads the lovers to a grim end. Schiller aimed his fire at court corruption and class pride alike. The play made such oppression fit for the stage as it had not been before. It remains the most performed of his early works.
galdos-trafalgar-bell-1884:
Benito Pérez Galdós began his Episodios Nacionales in 1873 with Trafalgar, and Clara Bell Englished it in 1884. The cycle grew to forty-six novels tracing Spain's nineteenth century. Gabriel Araceli, a cabin boy from Cádiz, tells this first tale from his old age.

Gabriel ships aboard the Santísima Trinidad at the battle of Trafalgar in 1805. Nelson's fleet, Spanish pride, and shattering cannon fire fill his boy's-eye view. Galdós mixes history with a servant's plain witness of great events. Bell's translation opened the cycle to English readers early. The series became Spain's national epic in prose, and Trafalgar is still its most read door.
clarin-la-regenta-1884:
Leopoldo Alas, who signed himself Clarín, published La Regenta in Spain in 1884 and 1885. The text here is the Spanish original; no English translation of the novel is in the public domain. Ana Ozores, wife of a retired judge in the provincial city of Vetusta, suffocates in piety, gossip, and boredom.

Two men circle her: her confessor, Fermín de Pas, and the local dandy Álvaro Mesía. Faith, ambition, and desire pull Ana toward a fall the whole town watches for. Clarín builds Vetusta street by street, soul by soul, with patient irony. Spanish readers rank La Regenta as their greatest novel of the nineteenth century. Its scale invites comparison with Madame Bovary and Anna Karenina.
kabbala-denudata-knorr-tome2-1684:
Knorr von Rosenroth issued the second tome of the Kabbala Denudata at Frankfurt in 1684, seven years after the first. The text is in Latin, like its predecessor. Tome two adds commentaries, further Zoharic treatises, and the Siphra de Zeniutha, the Book of Concealment, with the commentary ascribed to Luria's school.

The Siphra, a brief and dense Zoharic text on the divine kings before creation, anchors this volume's mysticism. Around it Knorr sets dissertations that argue Kabbalah and Christian doctrine toward each other. No English translation exists in the public domain. Together the two tomes formed early modern Europe's library of Kabbalah in one place. Christian Kabbalists cited Knorr for two centuries after.
zosimus-new-history-1684:
Zosimus, a pagan official at Constantinople, wrote his New History around 510 CE to explain why Rome was falling. The English text here is the anonymous version of 1684, the only one in the public domain. His six books run from Augustus to the sack of Rome in 410.

Zosimus blames the emperors who dropped the old gods, above all Constantine and Theodosius, for the empire's wounds. He gives the fullest narrative of the late empire's fall that survives. His voice is the last great pagan answer to Christian Rome. The old spelling of the 1684 print, with its long s, takes a page to get used to.
lotze-logic-bosanquet-1884:
Hermann Lotze, a German doctor turned philosopher, built his System of Philosophy in three parts, and the Logic came first. Bernard Bosanquet translated it for the Clarendon Press in 1884. The three books of the Logic treat thought, investigation, and knowledge in turn.

Lotze starts with the forms of thinking, concepts, judgments, and syllogisms, then asks how inquiry in law, history, and science really works. He ends with the question of what knowledge is and what it is worth. British idealists and the first analytic philosophers both learned from Lotze. Bosanquet's version was the form in which the English world read him.
lotze-metaphysic-bosanquet-1884:
The Metaphysic is the second part of Hermann Lotze's System of Philosophy, in Bernard Bosanquet's English version of 1884. Its three books treat ontology, cosmology, and psychology: what there is, how the world hangs together, and what the soul is. Lotze wrote as a trained doctor who refused to cut mind off from nature.

He argues that the mechanical order of science is real but not the whole truth: things act as they do because of what they are for. That blend of science and purpose made Lotze a bridge between German idealism and the new logic of his age. Bosanquet's translation spread his system through the English universities.
hartmann-philosophy-unconscious-vol1-188:
Eduard von Hartmann, a young German ex-officer, published his Philosophie des Unbewussten in 1869 and startled Europe. W C Coupland's English translation of 1884 fills three volumes, and volume one here treats the phenomenology of the unconscious. That is: Hartmann gathers the signs of unconscious mind at work in body, instinct, and feeling.

His claim is large: an unconscious will and idea steer nature and human life beneath our waking thought. Decades before Freud, Hartmann made the unconscious a central concept of philosophy. The first volume builds his case from reflex, instinct, and the healing wisdom of the body. It is a strange, powerful book that its century could not ignore.
hartmann-philosophy-unconscious-vol2-188:
Volume two of Coupland's 1884 Hartmann turns from the signs of the unconscious to its metaphysics, its inner nature and law. Eduard von Hartmann's Philosophy of the Unconscious, first published in German in 1869, argues that one unconscious principle works through all nature. Volume one had surveyed its effects; this volume asks what that principle is.

Hartmann joins Schopenhauer's blind will to Hegel's unfolding idea, and finds both at once in the unconscious. From atoms to human genius, one striving, knowing power drives the whole, on his account. The system swept Germany and reached England in Coupland's careful English. Volume two is where the bold architecture stands tallest.
hartmann-philosophy-unconscious-vol3-188:
Coupland's third volume of Hartmann, from 1884, carries the Philosophy of the Unconscious into religion and history. Eduard von Hartmann's German work of 1869 had grown through many editions into a system touching everything. Having traced the unconscious in nature and in mind, he now asks what it means for faith and for the fate of mankind.

Hartmann reads history as the unconscious slowly schooling humanity out of its illusions of happiness. Religion, on his view, moves through stages toward a clear-eyed, somber wisdom. His pessimism, argued at full scale, made him one of the most debated thinkers of his age. Volume three completes Coupland's English Hartmann, system and all.
spr-proceedings-vol2-1884:
Scholars and scientists founded the Society for Psychical Research in London in 1882. Volume two of its Proceedings, dated 1884, holds parts five through seven. The society set out to test claims of telepathy, apparitions, and trance speaking by strict methods. Its journal of record printed the evidence for all to judge.

Early thought transference trials fill many pages, with their scores and safeguards. Reports of apparitions arrive with names, dates, and cross checks. Sittings with mediums get the same hard treatment as lab work. Skeptical voices sit inside the society itself, by design. The volume shows a young field inventing its standards. Later debate kept returning to these records.
burnet-sacred-theory-of-the-earth-vol1-1:
Thomas Burnet's Sacred Theory of the Earth reached English readers in 1684. Volume one holds the two first books of his four part theory. The first book treats the Deluge, the second treats Paradise, the Earth as it first was. Burnet pictures the young Earth as smooth, fair, and without seas or mountains.

The Flood, in his telling, cracked that smooth shell and drowned the world. Ruined fragments of the crust became our mountains and ocean beds. The work founded modern catastrophist cosmology, Earth history by great sudden blows. Its grand style won readers across Europe for a century. The English translation spread the theory widely. Few books shaped early geology so much.
hering-condensed-materia-medica-1884:
Hering's guiding symptoms filled ten big volumes, and The Condensed Materia Medica of 1884 shrinks that wealth to pocket size. The second edition keeps Constantine Hering's marks and choices, so the strongest signs still stand out. A prescriber could carry the great man's life work in a coat pocket.

Condensing meant hard choices: only the symptoms Hering trusted most survive the cut. What remains reads like the distilled voice of the larger set, terse and ranked. Country doctors riding between patients prized such books, and this one ranks among the most portable forms of the great materia medica.
dorsey-omaha-sociology-1884:
James Owen Dorsey was a missionary turned ethnologist who knew the Omaha language deeply from years among the Omaha and Ponca. His 1884 report for the Bureau of American Ethnology describes how Omaha society was organized, down to its smallest rules.

Dorsey explains the gentes, the kin groups that fixed each person's duties, marriages, and place in the tribe. He describes the sacred tents and their holy objects, and the tribal circle, the camp arrangement that mapped the whole social order on the ground. His detail is dry but unmatched. Scholars still rely on this report for the structure of Siouan tribal life.
lang-custom-and-myth-1884:
Andrew Lang wrote these 1884 essays to defend a bold claim: that Greek and other classic myths began as the wild tales of early peoples. Against scholars who saw myth as high poetry spoiled, Lang saw survivals of savage custom and thought.

Essay by essay he takes up totemism, the bull-roarer used in secret rites, and the cruel or absurd elements in the tales of gods. He argues these oddities make sense once their origin in early ritual is seen. Lang wrote with wit and wide reading across folklore and anthropology. The book helped found the anthropological study of myth.
plos-pone-0003384:
Asish K. Ghosh and co-authors asked what a quiet gene does in normal cells in 2008. The gene makes MBP-1, a protein that turns other genes down. Extra MBP-1 was known to kill cancer cells and shrink tumors. But its day-to-day role in healthy cells was still unclear.

The team lowered MBP-1 levels in normal human skin cells called fibroblasts. Those cells then aged early, a state known as senescence. The aging ran through two guard proteins, p53 and p21. So normal levels of MBP-1 seem to hold cell aging back.
plos-pone-0003484:
Rubén Rabaneda-Bueno and co-authors studied mate-eating in a wild population for this 2008 paper. Sexual cannibalism pits female feeding gains against male survival. Females may gain more from eating a male than from mating with him. Males, in turn, may shun aggressive females.

In this natural population, cannibalism occurred at a high rate. The team measured the benefits that flowed to females. Eating mates brought real gains, not just a odd accident. The study weighs an extreme case of conflict between the sexes. Such findings test how far one sex will go at the other's expense.
plos-pone-0003584:
Sabine Telle and Marco Thines read DNA from old plant specimens in this 2008 methods paper. Herbarium sheets are dried plants kept for study, some very old. Molecular work on them had usually needed large amounts of material. The team worked with just two milligrams per sample.

They amplified a cox2 gene stretch of about 620 base pairs. Specimens up to 129 years old yielded readable DNA. Nineteen extraction methods and fifteen polymerases were compared. Museum collections thus become a time machine for plant evolution. Old sheets also hold species that are now extinct in the wild.
plos-pone-0003684:
Andrea C. Tricco, Jamie Brehaut, Maggie H. Chen, and colleagues published this research study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Cochrane reviews are trusted as careful summaries of medical evidence. Each one starts as a published protocol. No one had tracked how many of those protocols reach a finished review.

The authors followed 411 Cochrane protocols to see which ones were completed. They also looked for factors that predicted finishing. The audit measures the gap between starting a gold-standard review and publishing it, a gap that matters to everyone who funds or uses these reviews.
plos-pone-0003784:
Vera Halpern, Folasade Ogunsola, Orikomaba Obunge, and colleagues published this trial report in PLOS ONE in 2008. A vaginal gel that blocks HIV could give women a prevention method they control. The team ran a Phase III, double-blind, randomized trial in Nigeria of six percent cellulose sulfate gel.

The trial tested the gel's safety and its power to prevent male-to-female transmission of HIV. It also tracked gonorrhea and chlamydia infections. Big trials of this kind give the hard answers that smaller safety studies cannot, whatever the outcome turns out to be.
plos-pone-0003884:
Jack Kent and Andrea L. Meredith studied the brain clock in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Daily rhythms near 24 hours come from a small brain area called the suprachiasmatic nucleus. Clock genes inside its cells set the basic beat of that rhythm. Less was clear about how firing patterns of the cells add to timing.

The authors focused on BK channels, which help control when nerve cells fire. They found these channels shape the rhythm of bursts in the clock nucleus. The work links a single channel type to the pace of daily activity. It adds a cell-level piece to the story of how the brain keeps time.
plos-pone-0003984:
Eti Ben-Simon, Ilana Podlipsky, Amos Arieli, and co-authors studied the resting brain's alpha rhythm in 2008. Brain activity keeps changing even when a person rests. The alpha rhythm, at 8 to 12 hertz, marks that idle state. Whether it reflects one spot or a wide network was debated.

Their PLOS ONE article reports two alpha processes present at once. Both showed in recordings from resting human subjects. Two distinct rhythms suggest rest holds more than one active process. The result complicates the simple picture of an idling brain. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004084:
Daniel Oro, Antoni Margalida, Martina Carrete, and co-authors tested feeding sites for an endangered vulture in 2008. Conflicts with predators push many species toward extinction. Supplementary feeding at set sites is a popular simple fix. Such fixes can bring unforeseen conservation outcomes, though.

Their PLOS ONE article asks whether feeding truly boosts vulture viability. Feeding stations gather birds where food is predictable. Benefits must be weighed against risks like crowding and dependency. Evidence from this test guides vulture programs across Europe. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004184:
Arikuni Uchimura and colleagues published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. DNA polymerase delta is one of the main enzymes that copy DNA in eukaryotic cells, and it also helps repair and reshuffle DNA. Its working part, the p125 subunit, is encoded by the Pold1 gene. What this enzyme does for a developing mammal was not thoroughly known.

By disabling Pold1 in mice, the team shows that polymerase delta is required for early embryonic development. Embryos cannot get far without working DNA copying. The study pins a basic housekeeping enzyme to the very first chapter of life.
plos-pone-0004284:
Eun Chan Park, Doreen Glodowski, and Christopher Rongo published this neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Ubiquitination, the tagging of proteins, happens at synapses, yet its role there was unclear. Earlier work showed the ligase RPM-1 organises the sending side of junctions between nerve and muscle in the worm C. elegans.

Here the team find a novel postsynaptic role for RPM-1 in interneurons. Together with the p38 MAPK called PMK-3, it regulates trafficking of AMPA receptors, the main receivers of the excitatory signal glutamate. Moving receptors in and out of synapses is how brains tune connection strength.
plos-pone-0004384:
The H5N1 bird flu virus raised fears of a human pandemic. A vaccine that trains lasting, broad immunity would be a strong defense. Angelika Banzhoff, Roberto Gasparini, Franco Laghi-Pasini, and co-authors tested such a vaccine in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper covers adults in two age bands. One group was aged eighteen to sixty, the other over sixty.

The vaccine used an added booster ingredient called MF59. In total, 313 younger adults and 173 older adults took part. The authors report the shot built immune memory. It also raised antibodies that respond across differing strains, called heterotypic responses. Broad memory of that kind is what pandemic planners hope to bank ahead of time.
plos-pone-0004484: In 2009, Brenneis and Soppa found salt-lovers' RNA bookends essential. Translation regulation in salt-loving haloarchaea needed both UTR ends working as a pair. The RNA ends teamed up functionally. The finding maps archaeal gene control precisely. Both UTRs are truly essential.
plos-pone-0004584: In 2009, Morlan, Baker, and Sinicropi built a sharper mutation sniffer. Mutation detection by real-time PCR offered a simple, robust, highly selective method. The test spotted rare mutants fast. The method aids cancer diagnosis today. The neat approach is highly practical.
plos-pone-0004684: In 2009, He, Gitschier, and Zerjal mapped where HapMap volunteers' ancestors lived long ago. Geographical affinities of the HapMap samples were charted. The tricky ascertainment shaped the map strongly. The study informs population genetics research. The DNA samples were medical-genetic.
plos-pone-0004784: In 2009, Carpentier, Pierobon, and Hivroz built fake triggers for T cells anew. T-cell artificial focal triggering tools linked surface interactions with cell response.
