The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked.
frus-1945-50-intel-d384:
Secretary of State Acheson and Secretary of Defense Johnson sent a joint report to the National Security Council. The date was 1 July 1949. It stands as document 384 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950.

The form gathers work done by many hands into one text. It sets out the facts found, the points of doubt, and the course the writers advise. Joint reports from the two secretaries were rare. One sent to the Council carried the weight of both the State and Defense sides at once.
frus-1861-d84:
A further letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams is dated 14 September 1861. It is document 84 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward sent Adams two letters that day, on top of Adams's own dispatch home. The volume's London file swells at just this point of the autumn. It marks the season when the watch on Britain became a steady, daily duty rather than a crisis task. Autumn turned the London watch from a sprint into a siege of patience. A daily duty, well kept, is the least dramatic and most vital kind of service.
frus-1861-d184:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to Carl Schurz on 5 November 1861. The letter is document 184 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

When Seward was absent, Frederick W. Seward acted in his place as Assistant Secretary. His letter kept the Madrid line manned without a gap. It shows the office's depth: the work went on, in the same hand of style, whoever held the pen. Frederick Seward kept the pen until a wound in 1865 nearly cost him his life. The pen he kept in November served the office through four years of war.
frus-1861-d284:
Guidance for Mr. Haldeman left Washington on 30 July 1861, signed by William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 284 in the President's message volume for 1861. The letter comes from the first summer of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d84:
Guidance for Charles Francis Adams left Washington on 24 June 1862, signed by William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 84 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d184:
Document 184 completes the trio of Seward dispatches to London dated 4 November 1862 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. All three went to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister to Britain, in the same Atlantic mail.

By the time these letters reached London, Britain had decided against joining France in a truce proposal, though Adams did not yet know it. The file thus catches a strange overlap: orders written for a crisis already easing. Letters like this one show why envoys prized discretion alongside obedience in the age of slow mail. Seward trusted Adams's calm judgment and rarely overruled the man on the spot.
frus-1862-d284:
On 5 June 1862 William L. Dayton reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward from Paris, in a letter printed as Document 284 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Dayton's June reports reached a Washington deep in the Peninsula campaign, when every foreign reading of the war seemed to hang on Richmond. The Paris legation's value lay in its ear: what ministers said at dinner often mattered more than what they said in notes. This report adds one more week of that listening to the record Seward used. Policy at Napoleon III's court was made in private, so an envoy's ear mattered as much as his pen.
frus-1862-d384:
Simon Cameron, the American minister in Russia, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 23 July 1862, in a letter printed as Document 384 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Cameron wrote from St. Petersburg in the summer of the Union's discontent, when Richmond had been saved and foreign intervention was openly discussed in the west. Russia stood apart from that talk, and its envoy's reports carried that reassurance. This letter, sharing its date with a Seward dispatch, opens Cameron's run in the file. Cameron, a Pennsylvania political chief, had run the War Department before going to Russia. Letters to Russia favored broad lines of policy over fast-changing battle news.
frus-1862-d484:
James Shepherd Pike at The Hague received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 5 February 1862. It is Document 484 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

The Dutch were old hands at neutrality and maritime law, which made The Hague a useful listening post and a court worth keeping well informed. Seward's February order supplied Pike with the Union's account of the war at a moment of improving news from the West. Instructions like this one also fixed the exact words a minister could use on touchy points. The dispatch starts the year's two-way traffic in the Netherlands file.
frus-1862-d584:
Thomas Corwin wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward from Mexico on 24 March 1862, four days after his previous report. The letter is Document 584 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Fast reporting from Mexico City was justified that spring. The French advance moved week by week. So did the allied quarrel and the survival of the Juárez government. Corwin's letters gave Seward the material for the Union's careful public line, sympathy for Mexico without any promise of arms it could not keep. His reports also tracked Spanish conduct, which links this file to the Spanish documents printed later in the volume. The dispatch is one of a tight spring cluster from the war's most exposed American post.
frus-1862-d684:
William Sydney Thayer, the American consul general in Egypt, dated this dispatch 13 March 1862 and sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 684 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. Thayer had reported from Egypt through the fall and winter before.

By the spring of 1862 the war's trade shocks were plain in Egypt, where cotton planters rushed to feed the mills of Europe. Consular reports followed the boom and the strain it put on the land. Thayer's letter is one of those reports. It is the kind of ground-level news that let Washington judge how the war was reshaping trade far from the fight.
frus-1863p1-d84:
William H. Seward sent this second letter of 14 February 1863 to Charles Francis Adams in London. Adams held the American legation there. The letter is document 84 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Paired letters from Washington split the brief so Adams could act on each part in turn. This one follows its twin of the same date, with the stray 1862 sheet of the same day set before them both in the printing. The cluster is a small maze of dates, but the work is clear. Orders went out, claims were pressed, and a post was kept in step with home in the war's second winter.
frus-1863p1-d184:
The Secretary of State, William H. Seward, wrote to his minister in London, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, on 5 May 1863. The letter is document 184 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 5 letters between the same men dated that day.

Adams was told to deal chiefly with Lord John Russell, the foreign secretary. Seward's letters armed him with facts and wording for those meetings. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d284:
To guide his minister in London, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote these orders on 5 September 1863 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. They stand as document 284 of the 1863 volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

The chief aim behind such orders was simple: keep Britain from treating the Confederacy as a nation. Every instruction from Washington served that goal in some way. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d384:
On 7 February 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It appears as document 384 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Cases in these notes can look small, one ship or one arrested man, yet each tested the rules of neutrality. Both governments treated the precedents as serious business. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d484:
A 29 April 1863 dispatch from W. Hunter, chief clerk of the State Department reached Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863.

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d584:
The letter printed as document 584 was written on 13 July 1863 by Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d684:
F. W. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons on 4 November 1863. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, the man who spoke for London at the American capital. The letter is document 684 in Foreign Relations of the United States for 1863. F. W. Seward served at the State Department under his father.

Face-to-face ties in Washington mattered as much as the London mission. Lyons carried British views to the Lincoln team, and notes like this one carried the reply back. Each side tested the other's mood on the war, on trade, and on acts at sea. The reader sees that test in a short, formal note from the American side of the desk.
plos-pbio-0020384:
James A. Fraser, Stephanie Diezmann, Ryan L. Subaran, and their team compared sex-determining regions across kingdoms in PLOS Biology in 2004. In animals, sex chromosomes set sex. In some fungi, a mating-type region does a like job. The authors found these systems share surprising traits, a case of convergent evolution.

Both kinds of regions limit shuffling with their partner region, collect repeat DNA, and degrade over time. Those parallels arose on their own in each kingdom. They suggest any genome region that stops shuffling follows the same path of decay. The insight helps read the future of young sex chromosomes, including our own aging Y. It also guides work on fungal mating, which matters for crop disease.
plos-pone-0000184:
Jan A. van Gils, Vincent J. Munster, Reinder Radersma, and colleagues published this bird flu study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Swans infected with low-pathogenic avian influenza A virus, a mild strain, were tracked during migration. The authors found the infection hampered the birds' foraging and their migratory performance.

Even a mild infection can tax a bird that must feed heavily and fly far. The study quantifies that cost in wild swans. The results matter for predicting how bird flu moves with migration, since sick birds travel differently. They also reveal the hidden toll of low-grade infections in wild animals.
plos-pone-0000284:
Rajesh Kumar, Jing Qiu, Trupti Joshi, and colleagues published this rice genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It presents single feature polymorphism discovery in rice, a way to find DNA differences between rice varieties using microarray features rather than full sequencing. Each differing feature marks a spot where the varieties' genomes diverge.

Rice feeds half the world, and breeders need cheap markers to track traits. Polymorphism discovery by microarray offers markers at a fraction of sequencing cost. The authors demonstrate the approach in rice, adding tools for breeding programs that work with limited budgets.
plos-pone-0000384:
Yasuhiro Kitazoe and colleagues revisited one of evolution's dating disputes in PLOS ONE in 2007: when placental mammals first arose. Fossils and DNA-based clocks have given different answers, with DNA studies often pointing to a much older origin. The team set out to estimate the timing in a more robust way.

Molecular clocks convert DNA differences into years, but they are sensitive to how the math is done. By making the time estimates sturdier, the authors argue the two views can be reconciled. The paper matters because the age of the mammal family tree shapes how scientists explain the rise of mammals alongside, and after, the dinosaurs.
plos-pone-0000484:
Andreas Sundquist and colleagues reviewed a turning point in DNA sequencing, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. New high-throughput, short-read technologies could sequence DNA far faster and cheaper than older methods, but they produced millions of short fragments. The paper covered whole-genome sequencing and assembly with these technologies, the puzzle of stitching short reads into a genome.

Assembly is the hard part: short reads repeat and overlap ambiguously. Getting it right decides whether cheap sequencing is also trustworthy. Papers from this period mark a turning point. Genomics shifted from a few flagship projects to a routine tool. Any lab could now aim it at any organism.
plos-pone-0000584:
Leonid I. Brodsky and colleagues designed a method to find genes that matter in antiviral defense without prior guesses, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Their novel unsupervised method identifies genes important in the anti-viral response, and they applied it to patients receiving interferon and ribavirin for hepatitis C.

Unsupervised means the method finds its own patterns in the data rather than testing a preset list. In hepatitis C, only some patients respond to interferon therapy, and the gene signature of response was unclear. A method that surfaces the important genes could predict who benefits and reveal new drug targets.
plos-pone-0000684:
Gernot G. Supp, Alois Schlögl, Nelson Trujillo-Barreto and colleagues followed information flow in the brain during object recognition, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Familiar, meaningful objects reliably boost induced gamma-band responses in EEG recordings. These fast oscillations, above 30 hertz, appear at distinct scalp locations. They are thought to mark local cell groups forming on the fly.

The team analyzed the responses in the brain's source space, estimating where signals originate. Directed flow shows which areas drive which others as an object is recognized. That direction matters: recognition is not one area lighting up, but a conversation. Mapping its direction helps connect EEG patterns to real brain circuits.
plos-pone-0000784:
Brian J. North and Eric Verdin tracked a longevity-linked enzyme as it shuttles in and out of the nucleus, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Human SIRT2 is an NAD+-dependent protein deacetylase residing mainly in the cytoplasm, where it removes acetyl tags from tubulin, the cytoskeleton protein. They report SIRT2 keeps that cytoplasmic address during interphase by active nuclear export, in a manner dependent on the export machine Crm1.

During mitosis, its localization changes. An enzyme that moves between compartments can do different jobs at different cell stages. Sirtuins attract attention for roles in aging and metabolism, so mapping where SIRT2 sits, and when, is groundwork for that larger story.
plos-pone-0000884:
Janet Young, Hang Waters, Cora Dong and colleagues traced the decay of a smell gene across primate history, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The sense of smell rests on several subsystems, each tuned to its own set of chemical cues. In the main smell tissue, at least three types of sensing cells can be told apart by the genes they use.

One of those genes, for an enzyme called guanylyl cyclase D, has been breaking down in primates. The team followed that decline across species. A gene that fades this way tells a story about changing needs: as sight grew stronger in primates, some parts of smell may have mattered less.
plos-pone-0000984:
Sven Letourneau, Eung-Jun Im, Tumelo Mashishi and colleagues designed a universal HIV vaccine candidate and tested it before clinic, in PLOS ONE in 2007. HIV varies enormously, and that diversity can sink any single vaccine. A design that covers many variants at once was badly needed.

The team built an immunogen called HIV CONSV from the parts of the virus that change least across strains. Aiming T cells at conserved regions could give protection no matter which variant a person meets. Their paper covers the design and pre-clinical evaluation. Universal thinking, rather than strain chasing, is the paper's main bet.
plos-pone-0001084:
Tadashi Iwami, Osamu Kishida and Kinya Nishimura studied how salamander larvae offset the costs of a defense, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Animals often change several traits at once when danger looms, a package called phenotypic plasticity. The package arises from tangled ecological and physiological causes.

In Hynobius salamander larvae, an inducible defense brings costs. The team distinguish direct and indirect routes by which a compensatory phenotype develops and eases those costs. Compensation matters because a defense that bankrupts growth is no defense at all. Their analysis shows how trait packages are assembled, not just switched on. Pond predators made this system a sharp test case.
plos-pone-0001184:
Most CpG sites in mammal genomes carry methylation marks, but the CpG-rich stretches called CpG islands usually resist them, and nobody fully knows why. Shicai Fan, Fang Fang, and Xuegong Zhang searched the human genome for a clue, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They examined the boundaries of methylation-resistant CpG islands.

The authors found that binding sites for putative zinc finger proteins are over-represented at those boundaries. Zinc finger proteins grip DNA at specific sequences, so their clustering at island edges hints at a protective fence. Their result gives the methylation-resistance puzzle a concrete suspect to test.
plos-pone-0001284:
San Francisco has the highest tuberculosis rate in the United States, with recurrent outbreaks among homeless and marginally housed people. Brandon Higgs and colleagues studied how to detect outbreaks early in that population, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Outbreak detection trades off spatial resolution against temporal scale: finer geography can mean slower signals.

The authors analyze those trade-offs, building on syndromic surveillance work that uses patients' exact coordinates. For a disease that spreads in shelters and single-room hotels, knowing where to draw the detection boundary matters. Their study aims at earlier warnings for a hard-to-reach population.
plos-pone-0001384:
Francesc Garcia-Gonzalo and Juan Carlos Izpisúa Belmonte wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on human embryo stem cells. These cells can grow into many cell types, so they hold great hope for future cures. But labs still lack a clean, fixed food mix to grow them well. The pair studied fats bound to a common blood protein.

The authors show that these fats help the stem cells renew themselves and stay in their early state. That is a step toward defined growth mixes with no unknown parts. Such mixes are key for safe use in clinics. The work helps move stem cell growth from art toward a set, shared method.
plos-pone-0001484:
Hiroki Nakagawa and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a shared gene switch in mammals. About one in ten gene pairs sit head to head on facing DNA strands. A shared switch drives both genes, which often work as a pair. The team studied one such region, kept across species, between two named genes.

They mapped what turns this shared switch on and off. Kept regions like this tend to hold core control logic. The work shows how two genes can be tuned as a unit. That tuning helps cells keep paired jobs in step, a theme that recurs across the genome.
plos-pone-0001584:
Elizabeth Dinsdale and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on microbes at four coral atolls. Microbes run much of the life of both sound and worn coral reefs. The team sampled four atolls in the Northern Line Islands, from a tiny empty one to peopled ones. They mixed gene reads, scope work, cultures, and water tests.

Microbe mixes shifted sharply from the pristine atoll to the used ones. Human use left a clear mark in the unseen life of the reef. Those marks may warn of reef decline before coral loss shows. The set forms a base line for reef health work.
plos-pone-0001684:
Jianwei Jiao, Akira Nakajima, William G. M. Janssen, and their co-authors linked one brain receptor to how practice improves movement, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Motor skills are learned by training, and genes and environment are thought to interact in that learning. The receptor is NR2B, a part of the NMDA receptor, a key molecular switch for learning in the brain.

Working with cerebellar granule cells, the team reports that NR2B expression specifically helps motor training improve motor learning. The full text gives the training tests, the brain measurements, and the comparison across animal groups. The cerebellum fine-tunes movement. A receptor there that gates the benefit of practice helps explain why the same training yields different gains in different learners.
plos-pone-0001784:
Anilkumar Pillai studied brain tissue from people with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder in a 2008 PLOS ONE research report. Current theories blame altered brain plasticity: reduced nerve cell growth and migration, slow myelin growth, and abnormal synapse reshaping. BDNF, a growth factor for neurons, had shown changes in schizophrenia.

Pillai measured Sprouty2, a regulator of growth factor signaling, in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and found lower Sprouty2 levels in both, tied to BDNF levels. The full text gives the tissue readings and the strength of the link. Linked changes in a growth factor and its brake support the plasticity theory. They also mark a pathway that treatments might aim to restore.
plos-pone-0001884:
Sara Batelli and colleagues studied two proteins tied to Parkinson disease in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. In this illness, brain cells die off slowly, and clumps of a protein called alpha-synuclein are a hallmark. A second protein, DJ-1, is linked to rare family forms of the disease, but its exact job was unclear.

The team used a cell model of oxidative stress, the kind of chemical strain thought to harm brain cells in this disease. They report that DJ-1 shifts the clumping state of alpha-synuclein, and that a heat-shock helper protein, HSP70, plays a part. The link gives drug work a fresh target: keep the clumps from forming.
plos-pone-0001984:
Charles Shelburne and co-authors found a blood sign that predicts gum health in at-risk patients, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Periodontitis is a chronic gum infection tied to the bacterium Porphyromonas gingivalis. Helper proteins called chaperones keep other proteins in shape and also act as strong immune targets.

The team measured antibodies in blood against one chaperone from this bacterium, called HtpG. As the title states, those antibodies predict health in patients prone to gum disease. A blood marker that flags who stays healthy could guide how often at-risk patients need care, and which ones need more.
plos-pone-0002084:
Laurent Bogdanik and co-authors studied a muscle protein at the fly's nerve-muscle junction, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The dystrophin-glycoprotein complex links a muscle fiber's inner frame to the matrix outside it, guarding the fiber from strain. One part, dystroglycan, sits in that complex in muscle.

The team asked what dystroglycan does at the synapse itself, in the fruit fly. As the title states, muscle dystroglycan organizes the postsynapse and regulates how much neurotransmitter the nerve side releases. A protein known for muscle strength thus also tunes talk between nerve and muscle.
plos-pone-0002184:
Kristen Barthel and Xuedong Liu reported a surprise hiding place for a gene switch, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The human genome holds only about 25,000 genes, far too few to explain human complexity on their own. Much of the answer lies in how genes are regulated, and switches called enhancers are a big part of that control.

Enhancers are usually found outside genes. The team found one inside the coding region of ADAMTS5, a gene whose protein cuts other proteins outside cells. A switch buried in a gene's own text blurs the line between code and control. The find adds to the case that gene regulation is layered and dense.
plos-pone-0002284:
Mao Chen and co-authors reviewed whether Bt crop plants harm the insects that attack crop pests, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Transgenic plants that make crystal toxins from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis kill target pests, and their ecological safety is still debated. Much of that debate centers on non-target organisms, above all the parasitoid wasps that naturally control pests.

The authors critically assessed the studies on Bt plants and parasitoids. Parasitoids can meet the toxin through the hosts they live in, so effects may be indirect. A clear-eyed review helps regulators weigh real risks to the farmer's smallest allies against the gains of pest control.
plos-pone-0002384:
Research by Greene and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Justin M. Greene, Benjamin J. Burwitz, Alex J. Blasky, and others. Its subject is allogeneic Lymphocytes Persist and Traffic in Feral MHC-Matched Mauritian Cynomolgus Macaques. Thus far, live attenuated SIV has been the most successful method for vaccinating macaques against pathogenic SIV challenge; however.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002484:
Jiang and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Hongying Jiang, Jigar J. Patel, Ming Yi, and others. Its subject is genome-Wide Compensatory Changes Accompany Drug- Selected Mutations in the Plasmodium falciparum crt Gene. Mutations in PfCRT (Plasmodium falciparum chloroquine-resistant transporter), particularly the substitution at amino acid position 76, confer chloroquine (CQ) resistance in P.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002584:
Led by Medina, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Reinhold J. Medina, Christina L. O'Neill, Adrian B. Devine, and others. Its subject is the Pleiotropic Effects of Simvastatin on Retinal Microvascular Endothelium Has Important Implications for Ischaemic Retinopathies. Current guidelines encourage the use of statins to reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease in diabetic patients.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002684:
Work by Marc-André Prost and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was implication of new WHO growth standards on identification of risk factors and estimated prevalence of malnutrition in rural malawian infants. Authorship is credited in the record to Marc-André Prost and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. The World Health Organization (WHO) released new Child Growth Standards in 2006 to replace the current National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) growth reference. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002784:
Work by Steven D. Wiederman and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was a model for the detection of moving targets in visual clutter inspired by insect physiology. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Steven D. Wiederman, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. We present a computational model for target discrimination based on intracellular recordings from neurons in the fly visual system. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002884:
Tali Sharot, Matthew L. Davidson, Meredith M. Carson and co-authors tested in 2008 whether eye movements can predict rich recall. A past item can feel vividly remembered, with its setting brought back to mind, or merely familiar. Earlier work hinted that more focus at first sight leads to the richer kind of memory later.

In the PLOS ONE study, how the eyes moved while people first saw items was tracked against later reports of remembering versus just knowing. The title states that eye movements did predict the richer experience. Memory researchers get a simple outward sign of how deep a memory is being laid down.
plos-pone-0002984:
Anders Løbner-Olesen, Monika Slominska-Wojewodzka, Flemming Hansen and co-authors profiled E. coli cells blocked from starting DNA copying in 2008. Starting chromosome replication needs the proteins DnaA and DnaC, and faulty versions are often used to synchronize cell populations. The team focused on the dnaC mutant.

Using DNA microarrays, they measured RNA levels in cells unable to initiate replication. Inactivation of DnaC induced the SOS response, the cell's DNA damage alarm, plus genes for building nucleotides. Published in PLOS ONE, the profile shows how tightly copying, damage control, and raw materials are linked. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003084:
Manuel Gonçalves, Maarten Holkers, Gijsbert van Nierop and co-authors targeted large DNA inserts to chosen chromosome sites in 2008. A prominent gene therapy goal is vehicles that integrate added DNA at specific loci. That precision would prevent insertional cancer risk and provide long-term expression of the therapeutic gene.

Their system uses a fiber-modified, high-capacity adenovirus-based vector to insert large DNA into the human genome at targeted spots. Published in PLOS ONE, capacity plus targeting is a rare pairing. It speaks to therapies needing whole genes, not just small patches. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003184:
Tiny Boumans, Sharon M. H. Gobes, Colline Poirier and colleagues image songbird brains hearing sounds in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Male songbirds learn their songs from an adult tutor when young. A network of brain nuclei called the song system is the likely base for learning and producing song, but the networks that process auditory feedback signals were less clear.

Using functional MRI of auditory responses in the zebra finch forebrain, the team find a hierarchy based on signal strength but not selectivity. Readers learn how hearing areas are organized in a bird that learns by listening. The results inform wider work on learning complex sounds, including speech.
plos-pone-0003284:
Aki P. Järvinen, Jukka Hiissa, Laura L. Elo and colleagues predict genetic interactions in yeast in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Despite new lab techniques for changing multiple genes and measuring their effects on traits, genetic interactions have remained very hard to predict on a large scale. The team use a recent high-resolution screen of genetic interactions in yeast as their basis.

They propose predicting quantitative genetic interactions by means of sequential matrix approximation. Readers get a shortcut by computer for a huge test space, since gene pairs grow far faster than labs can test them. Good predictions let labs spend their tests on the pairs most likely to matter.
plos-pone-0007384: Infectious bronchitis virus is a coronavirus that sickens chickens, and its replicase gene — the machinery the virus uses to copy itself — was found to shape how harmful the infection becomes. The team had already shown that swapping the spike gene between harmless and dangerous strains changes which cells the virus enters. This work shows the replicase gene independently decides how severe the disease is.
plos-pone-0007484: Between 1997 and 2006, unplanned short hospital stays for children in England rose sharply. puysegur-memoires-magnetisme-animal-1784:
The Marquis de Puységur, a French noble and follower of Mesmer, published his Mémoires on animal magnetism in 1784. Treating a young peasant on his estate, he stumbled on something Mesmer had missed. His patient fell not into convulsions but into a calm, sleep-like trance.

Puységur called the state artificial somnambulism. In it, patients spoke, answered, and seemed to read their own illnesses. His reports shifted attention from Mesmer's fluid to the patient's mind. That turn points toward hypnosis and later talk-based cures. The Mémoires are the hinge between mesmerism as physics and the study of the inner life.
bailly-rapport-commissaires-magnetisme-a:
In 1784 the French king set a royal commission to test Mesmer's animal magnetism. Jean-Sylvain Bailly drafted its report, and Benjamin Franklin, Antoine Lavoisier, and Joseph Guillotin were among its signers. The commission ran careful trials, blindfolding patients and swapping magnetized objects for plain ones.

The verdict was firm. No fluid could be found, and the effects came from imagination alone. The report is a landmark of scientific testing, a debunking carried out with wit and rigor. It did not end mesmerism, but it set the standard for judging such claims. Enlightenment reason speaks here at its most decisive.
societe-royale-medecine-rapport-magnetis:
